h1: Shoulder Joint Anatomy: Glenohumeral Labrum, Rotator Cuff and Bursa
blurb: Why the shallow ball-and-socket glenohumeral joint achieves 360-degree reach, stabilized by the fibrocartilaginous labrum and four SITS rotator cuff tendons.
lead: Shaped like a golf ball resting on a shallow tee, the glenohumeral shoulder joint trades bony depth for unmatched mobility—relying on a muscular cuff to stay centered. This illustrated study guide examines 20 documented anatomical entries—including Supraspinatus tendon, Infraspinatus tendon, Teres minor tendon—connecting visible form, tissue organization, and physiological function.

Cut-away view of the cuff, labrum, capsule and biceps tendon — the structures behind most shoulder clinics.

When you trace how shoulder joint anatomy functions in the living body, each documented landmark contributes a specific mechanical or physiological step. Key structures covered in this guide include Supraspinatus tendon (initiates abduction (first 15°)), Infraspinatus tendon (external rotation), Teres minor tendon (external rotation + capsule tension), and Subscapularis tendon (internal rotation; anterior stability). By following all 20 illustrated landmarks in sequence, you can see how gross morphology, internal chambers or layers, and surrounding vessels work as one integrated unit.

Understanding these structural relationships is essential for both anatomy exams and real-world physiological reasoning. Practical anatomical correlations also stand out: for supraspinatus tendon, most torn cuff tendon — painful arc 60–120°; for infraspinatus tendon, tear → weak external rotation. questions.question: Why can the shoulder move so freely?
questions.answer: The shallow glenoid cavity permits a wide range of movement. The labrum, capsule, rotator cuff and surrounding muscles help stabilize the humeral head. In relation to glenoid fossa, this structure receives humeral head in shoulder joint.

questions.question: Which muscles form the rotator cuff?
questions.answer: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis form the rotator cuff around the glenohumeral joint. In relation to teres minor tendon, this structure external rotation + capsule tension. From an anatomical and functional standpoint, part of cuff tears in overhead athletes.

questions.question: What is the supraspinatus tendon?
questions.answer: Over the top of the humeral head. Function: Initiates abduction (first 15°). In relation to supraspinatus tendon, this structure initiates abduction (first 15°). From an anatomical and functional standpoint, most torn cuff tendon — painful arc 60–120°.

questions.question: Where is the teres minor tendon located?
questions.answer: Below infraspinatus. Function: External rotation + capsule tension. In relation to teres minor tendon, this structure external rotation + capsule tension. From an anatomical and functional standpoint, part of cuff tears in overhead athletes.

questions.question: What is the function of the glenoid labrum?
questions.answer: Function: Adds ~50% of glenoid depth. Fibrocartilage rim deepening the socket. In relation to glenoid labrum, this structure adds ~50% of glenoid depth. From an anatomical and functional standpoint, SLAP lesions in throwers; Bankart in dislocation.
